newsitem.title: CROATIA: Belgian UN soldier shot in Serb enclave of Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Belgian UN soldier shot in Serb enclave of Croatia.

text.p: A Belgian corporal was killed and two other U.N. officials were injured in a shooting incident in the Serb-controlled town of Vukovar in eastern Croatia on Friday, a United Nations spokesman said.

"An investigation was initiated and the U.N. and the Transitional Police Force (TPF) arrested the suspect," Philip Arnold, spokesman for the U.N. Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), told a news conference.
This was the first U.N. soldier to be killed, except in traffic accidents, since the U.N. mission took control of the area in spring 1996.
A Jordanian soldier and an UNTAES civilian officer wounded in the shooting were taken to the Vukovar hospital. The nationality of the latter has not been disclosed.
The incident occurred at 10.30 a.m. (0930 GMT) on the main road about a kilometre (half a mile) from the UNTAES headquarters in Vukovar, Arnold said.
Vukovar is the biggest town in the Serb-held region of Eastern Slavonia which is due to return to Croatian government rule by mid-June.
The town was devastated during the Croatian war for independence when Serb forces backed by the Yugoslav army laid siege to Vukovar and pounded it with artillery.
"The situation is contained," Arnold quoted the UNTAES military commander, Belgian Major-General Willie Hanset, as saying.
Hanset said the incident has "necessitated initiating control measures" but did not elaborate.
Arnold said the measures might have been a part of an attempt to arrest the suspect.
Another U.N. source, who asked not to be named, said there were some difficulties crossing from one part of the enclave to another earlier on Friday: "There seems to be some restriction of movement."

A series of incidents in the last month have raised tensions in the area where the local Serb population is getting increasingly nervous as the deadline for the "peaceful reintegration" of the region into Croatia approaches.
A Roman Catholic church in Ilok was bombed, Croatian offices for issuing documents and paying out pensions were stoned on several occasions.
Arnold said four of 23 Croatian administrative offices were temporarily closed due to opposition by the ethnic Serb population.
Local elections, in which Serbs will vote for the representatives of municipal bodies under Croatian law, are scheduled for mid-March.
